ai.definition: Photosynthesis is a natural process used by plants, algae, and some bacteria to convert light energy from the sun into chemical energy stored in molecules like glucose. This process involves capturing sunlight using chlorophyll and converting it into sugars through a series of reactions.
ai.howItWorks: During photosynthesis, chlorophyll within plant cells absorbs sunlight, which is then used to split water molecules (H₂O) and convert carbon dioxide (CO₂) into glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆). This process releases oxygen as a byproduct. The chemical energy stored in the bonds of glucose fuels various life processes.
ai.problemSolved: Photosynthesis solves the challenge of efficiently converting sunlight into usable chemical energy, which is essential for supporting complex ecosystems and nearly all forms of life on Earth.
ai.manufacturing: Not applicable; photosynthesis occurs naturally within living organisms without human intervention or manufacturing processes.
ai.costDrivers: No direct costs associated with the natural process of photosynthesis. However, factors such as environmental conditions (light, water, CO₂ levels) can influence its efficiency and productivity.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Research is ongoing to improve artificial photosynthesis technologies that could potentially enhance or replicate this natural process for industrial applications like renewable energy production.
ai.regulation: Not applicable; being a natural biological process, there are no regulatory requirements associated with photosynthesis itself.
ai.risks: Environmental risks include overuse of land for agriculture, which can lead to deforestation and loss of biodiversity. There is also the risk of introducing genetically modified organisms (GMOs) that could have unintended ecological consequences.
ai.profitability: Not applicable; as a natural process, photosynthesis does not generate revenue or profit in the traditional sense but supports all life on Earth indirectly through energy provision.
ai.futureDevelopment: Research is focused on developing artificial photosynthesis technologies to mimic and improve upon nature's processes. These efforts aim to create more efficient methods for producing renewable fuels and chemicals using sunlight.

glossary.def: A green pigment found in plant cells that absorbs light energy from the sun, crucial for photosynthesis.
The process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert sunlight into chemical energy stored in sugars like glucose.

subsystems.name: Light-harvesting antenna
subsystems.role: captures sunlight and funnels the energy toward the reaction centres.

subsystems.name: Water-splitting centre
subsystems.role: uses captured light to tear electrons out of water, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

subsystems.name: Electron transport and energy currency
subsystems.role: moves electrons along a chain and converts the resulting proton gradient into ATP and NADPH.

subsystems.name: Carbon-fixing cycle
subsystems.role: spends ATP and NADPH to turn CO₂ into sugars.

subsystems.name: Leaf plumbing and gas exchange
subsystems.role: supplies CO₂ and water and ships the sugar out to the rest of the plant.

subsystems.name: Storage and growth
subsystems.role: banks the captured energy as biomass — the usable output.

buildSteps.title: Build the chloroplast
buildSteps.detail: A plant cell assembles the organelle that hosts the light reactions; most of its proteins are imported from the cell nucleus, and the chloroplasts then divide on their own.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the light-harvesting membranes
buildSteps.detail: Chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments are bound to proteins and inserted into stacked thylakoid membranes, where each antenna complex is tuned to catch a slightly different band of light.

buildSteps.title: Install the water-splitting catalyst
buildSteps.detail: A manganese–calcium–oxygen cluster is built at the heart of Photosystem II; because light constantly damages it, the plant rebuilds it continuously.

buildSteps.title: Wire the electron chain
buildSteps.detail: Electrons travel from Photosystem II through plastoquinone and cytochrome b6f to Photosystem I, and the proton gradient this creates drives ATP synthase.

buildSteps.title: Stock the carbon-fixing cycle
buildSteps.detail: RuBisCO and the other Calvin-cycle enzymes are loaded into the stroma; plants in hot, dry places add pumps (C4 and CAM pathways) that concentrate CO₂ first so the enzyme works better.

buildSteps.title: Grow the panel
buildSteps.detail: Leaves expand to expose a large, thin surface to the sun; stomata open to admit CO₂ while veins deliver water and carry sugar away.

buildSteps.title: Bank and ship the product
buildSteps.detail: Sugars are stored as starch or exported as sucrose through the phloem, feeding growth and becoming the biomass we harvest.

buildSteps.title: Improve the design
buildSteps.detail: Breeding and genetic engineering are used to speed up RuBisCO, cut wasteful reactions, and move C4 machinery into crops that lack it.

prerequisites.why: chlorophyll and related molecules capture photons across roughly 400–700 nm of the visible spectrum.
the manganese cluster in Photosystem II does this at room temperature; human-made equivalents are only partial.
RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle build sugars from carbon dioxide, though the enzyme is slow and easily confused by oxygen.
the thylakoid membrane separates charge and stores energy, which is how light is converted into chemical energy.
we can edit single enzymes in crops but cannot yet rebuild the whole system from scratch.
no built system yet matches plants at turning sunlight, water and CO₂ into fuel at scale.

pathway.milestone: forests, crops and algae running photosynthesis worldwide
pathway.unlocks: food, biomass, wood and first-generation biofuels.

pathway.milestone: crops engineered for higher photosynthetic efficiency, including shortcuts around wasteful reactions and efforts to install C4 photosynthesis in rice
pathway.unlocks: more food and biomass per hectare of land and litre of water.

pathway.milestone: cultivated algae and cyanobacteria in ponds and closed photobioreactors
pathway.unlocks: fuels, animal feed and chemicals grown on non-farm land.

pathway.milestone: artificial photosynthesis — sunlight, water and CO₂ converted directly into hydrogen, methanol or other fuels in engineered cells or reactors
pathway.unlocks: liquid and gaseous fuels made without farmland, if efficiency and durability can be solved.
